column1: Information theory|broad_field|idea|shannon|Introduction, pp. 1–2|Measure communication choices without treating message meaning as the engineering quantity.|local:authored:000609|Same established field of quantified information and communication limits.|

Data compression|topic|idea|deflate|Abstract; §2|Reduce representation size by replacing repeated strings and assigning economical symbol codes.|Q2493|Same broad encoding-with-fewer-bits meaning; DEFLATE supplies a concrete example.|

Huffman coding|idea|idea|deflate|§3.2.1|Assign variable-length prefix codes using symbol frequencies to minimize expected code length.|Q2493|Data compression is the general goal; Huffman coding is a particular frequency-based coding construction.|

Prefix-free code|idea|idea|deflate|§3.2.1|Decode concatenated codewords unambiguously because no codeword is another codeword's prefix.|Q2493|General compression does not identify the prefix restriction that permits instantaneous symbol decoding.|Prefix code

Canonical Huffman coding|facet_or_application|idea|deflate|§3.2.2|Reconstruct a Huffman codebook from ordered code lengths using deterministic code assignment.|Q2493|This is a codebook-representation method, distinct from general compression and from selecting Huffman lengths.|

LZ77|idea|idea|deflate|§2; §3.2.5|Replace repeated byte strings with backward distance and length references within a sliding history.|Q2493|General compression does not specify dictionary backreferences, which differ from frequency-based symbol coding.|Lempel–Ziv 77

DEFLATE|idea|idea|deflate|Abstract; §2|Combine LZ77 references and Huffman-coded symbols inside a lossless block format.|Q2493|The named interoperable format is a specific composition of methods, not the broad compression identity.|Deflate

Dynamic Huffman blocks in DEFLATE|facet_or_application|idea|deflate|§3.2.6–§3.2.7|Transmit block-specific code lengths rather than always using the format's fixed Huffman tables.|Q2493|Block-specific codebook transmission is a supported format choice, distinct from the general format or Huffman algorithm.|

Unicode normalization|idea|idea|normalization|§1.2–§1.3|Transform equivalent character sequences into a common binary representation through decomposition, ordering, and optional recomposition.|Q494756|Data is the broad representation category; normalization is a specified equivalence-preserving text transformation.|

Canonical equivalence in Unicode|facet_or_application|idea|normalization|§1.1, Figure 1|Recognize a precomposed accented character and its decomposed sequence as the same abstract character.|Q494756|This formal equivalence relation concerns alternative text encodings, not data in general or sociological normalization.|

Compatibility equivalence in Unicode|facet_or_application|idea|normalization|§1.1, Figure 2; §1.2 warning|Treat certain stylistic or presentation variants as equivalent while recognizing potentially meaningful distinctions lost by folding.|Q494756|Weaker compatibility equivalence can erase distinctions that canonical equivalence preserves.|

Normalization across string concatenation|facet_or_application|idea|normalization|§1.4, Table 2|Recheck normalization at concatenation boundaries because joining normalized strings can require reordering or composition.|Q494756|This is a closure failure of normalization under concatenation, not another name for normalization itself.|

UTF-8|idea|idea|utf8|§2–§3|Encode Unicode scalar values in one to four bytes while preserving ASCII byte values.|Q494756|A defined variable-length text encoding is narrower than the baseline's general computing-data category.|

Overlong UTF-8 encodings|facet_or_application|idea|utf8|§3; §10|Reject longer-than-permitted encodings so alternate byte sequences cannot bypass character-based security checks.|local:catalog:encoding-specificity|The baseline concept concerns memory retrieval cues; this is invalid text encoding and parser security.|

Unicode code point|idea|idea|utf8|§3, encoding definition|Distinguish the integer assigned to a character from the bytes used by an encoding.|Q494756|An abstract numeric character position is distinct from its storage encoding and from data generally.|

Grapheme cluster|idea|idea|segmentation|§3, introductory discussion and Table 1a|Group code points into a best-effort approximation of a user-perceived character for text editing.|Q5597119|Graphetics studies written forms; grapheme clusters are an implementable Unicode segmentation unit.|Extended grapheme cluster

Binary search|idea|idea|queryplanner|§1.2–§1.3|Exploit sorted keys to find a record with logarithmic rather than full-scan search effort.|Q8513|A database is the collection; binary search is a general ordered-search procedure used to retrieve records.|

Covering index|facet_or_application|idea|queryplanner|§1.7|Include search and output columns in an index so a query need not consult the original table.|Q8513|Distinct from a database generally and from indexes that still require table lookups.|

Multi-column index|facet_or_application|idea|queryplanner|§1.6|Order index entries by several columns so combined constraints avoid filtering unrelated intermediate matches.|Q8513|Composite key ordering is an indexing technique, not a paraphrase of a database or covering-index property.|Composite index

A Mathematical Theory of Communication|topic|named_subject|shannon|Title; Introduction, pp. 1–2|See how Shannon's 1948 paper separated message selection from semantics to formulate an engineering theory.|local:authored:000609|The specific published work differs from the broader field it helped establish.|

Distributed systems|broad_field|idea|raft|§2, replicated state machines|Coordinate machines through messages while preserving shared results despite some machine failures.|local:authored:000520|Same networked-computation field; replicated state machines provide the concrete example.|

Database|topic|idea|sqliteabout|About SQLite, main explanatory paragraphs|Organize related tables and indexes so stored information can be queried and updated consistently.|Q8513|Same organized-computing-data meaning; SQLite illustrates its implementation.|

SQL|topic|idea|queryplanner|Overview; §1.1–§1.3|Describe desired query results declaratively while a database planner chooses how to find them.|Q8513|SQL is a query language; a database is the collection it operates on.|Structured Query Language

SQLite|topic|named_subject|sqliteabout|About SQLite, first two main paragraphs|Embed a transactional database directly in an application without a separate database server process.|Q8513|The particular software library is distinct from the general database concept.|

Atomic commit|idea|idea|atomiccommit|§1 Introduction|Make a transaction appear all-or-nothing even though storage writes happen sequentially and can be interrupted.|Q8513|A transaction completion guarantee is narrower than a database and distinct from concurrent-read isolation.|

Rollback journal|idea|idea|sqliteisolation|Isolation And Concurrency, rollback mode|Preserve old database content before overwrite so an uncompleted transaction can be undone.|Q8513|The recovery mechanism stores prior pages, whereas write-ahead logging appends new changes.|

Write-ahead logging|idea|idea|wal|§2 How WAL Works|Append committed changes separately before transferring them into the main database, allowing concurrent readers.|Q8513|A logging architecture is distinct from the database category and rollback journals that preserve old content.|WAL

Snapshot isolation|idea|idea|sqliteisolation|Isolation And Concurrency, WAL example|Give a read transaction a stable historical view while later commits remain invisible until it restarts.|local:catalog:serializable-snapshot-isolation|The baseline adds conflict checking to ensure serializability; ordinary snapshot isolation is the underlying consistent-read mechanism.|

WAL checkpointing|facet_or_application|idea|wal|§2.1 Checkpointing|Move committed log content into the database as a separate operation from reading, writing, and committing.|Q8513|Checkpointing is the log-to-database transfer phase, not another name for writing a log.|

Replicated state machine|idea|idea|raft|§2|Execute the same ordered commands deterministically on several replicas to obtain matching states and outputs.|local:authored:000520|This replication model is one way to implement distributed systems, not the entire field.|

Raft consensus algorithm|idea|idea|raft|§4–§5|Separate leader election, log replication, and safety to make a replicated-log consensus algorithm easier to understand.|local:authored:000520|Raft is a specific designed algorithm rather than the general distributed-systems field.|Raft

Distributed consensus|idea|idea|raft|§2; §5|Make non-Byzantine replicas agree on ordered commands, with availability requiring a communicating majority.|Q5162845|The baseline describes general multi-agent decision dynamics; this proposal is crash-fault-tolerant replicated-log agreement with an explicit failure model.|Consensus algorithm

Randomized election timeouts|facet_or_application|idea|raft|§5.2|Spread election starts probabilistically so competing candidates are less likely to repeatedly split votes.|local:authored:000520|This is a leader-election liveness technique, distinct from replication or distributed computation generally.|

Joint consensus in Raft|facet_or_application|idea|raft|§6, pp. 10–11|Require separate old- and new-configuration majorities during membership changes to prevent incompatible simultaneous majorities.|Q5162845|This is a particular safe membership-transition protocol, not general collective consensus dynamics.|

Replicated log|idea|idea|raft|§2; §5.3|Retain an ordered command history across replicas and repair disagreements before applying committed entries.|local:authored:000520|The durable ordered record is distinct from the deterministic execution model that consumes it.|Log replication

HTTP method idempotency|idea|idea|http|§9.2.2|Distinguish repeated intended effects from identical responses or the absence of incidental logging.|local:catalog:http-idempotency|Same HTTP method property already reviewed in the baseline; retain its canonical identity.|HTTP idempotence

HTTP entity tag|idea|idea|http|§8.8.3|Use an opaque representation validator to detect changes without requiring clients to understand its construction.|local:catalog:http-if-match-lost-update-prevention|An entity tag is the validator; the baseline is one conditional-update application of it.|ETag;Entity tag

HTTP If-Match update preconditions|facet_or_application|idea|http|§13.1.1|Apply a state-changing request only when its representation tag still matches, preventing intervening updates from being overwritten.|local:catalog:http-if-match-lost-update-prevention|Same conditional-update meaning and documented use case as the baseline; reuse existing ID.|

TCP slow start|facet_or_application|idea|tcp|§3.1|Probe available network capacity by increasing outstanding data as acknowledgments arrive until a threshold or congestion intervenes.|local:authored:000520|A transport congestion-control phase is distinct from general networked computation.|

TCP congestion window|idea|idea|tcp|§2; §3.1|Limit unacknowledged sending with a network-congestion bound separate from the receiver's advertised capacity.|local:authored:000520|The sender's congestion bound is distinct from receiver flow control and the broader distributed-systems field.|cwnd

Computer security|broad_field|idea|saltzerintro|Abstract; Glossary, Security and Protection|Control who can use or modify stored information through architectural protection and authentication mechanisms.|Q3510521|Same protection-of-computer-systems meaning as the registered concept.|

Cryptography|broad_field|idea|tls|§1; §2; Appendix E|Combine keyed encryption and authentication to protect message confidentiality, integrity, and peer identity.|local:authored:000527|Same field and cryptographic goals as the earlier card; retain registered ID.|

Principle of least privilege|idea|idea|saltzer|§I.A, principle f|Give each program and user only necessary permissions to limit accidents and the code requiring trust.|Q3510521|The minimum-authority design principle is a narrower mechanism within computer security.|Least privilege

Fail-safe defaults|idea|idea|saltzer|§I.A, principle b|Deny access unless a permission rule explicitly allows it so missing rules tend to fail closed.|Q3510521|The default authorization decision is distinct from the broader security field.|

Complete mediation|idea|idea|saltzer|§I.A, principle c|Check authority for every access, including recovery and maintenance paths rather than only ordinary operation.|Q3510521|This is a coverage requirement for access checks, separate from default denial or minimum permissions.|

Separation of privilege|idea|idea|saltzer|§I.A, principle e|Require independently held authorities so one error or compromised party cannot alone unlock a protected action.|Q7451821|Separating mechanism from policy concerns design layers; separation of privilege concerns multiple required authorities.|

Open security design|idea|idea|saltzer|§I.A, principle d|Keep protection dependent on guarded keys rather than secrecy of the mechanism, enabling public review.|Q3510521|Public inspectability of design is distinct from general security and from disclosing secret keys.|Open design

Economy of mechanism|idea|idea|saltzer|§I.A, principle a|Keep protection mechanisms small and simple to make hidden access paths easier to examine.|Q3510521|This security simplicity principle is distinct from economic organizations and from minimum privilege.|

Capability-based security|idea|idea|saltzerintro|Glossary, Capability and Ticket-oriented|Represent authority with unforgeable object-specific tickets that a principal presents to obtain access.|Q3510521|Capabilities encode authority in possession of a ticket, unlike an object's list of permitted principals.|Capability security

Access control list|idea|idea|saltzerintro|Glossary, Access control list and List-oriented|Associate an object with a list of principals authorized to access it.|Q3510521|Object-centered permission lists differ from principal-held capabilities and from security generally.|ACL

Password salting|facet_or_application|idea|nist|§3.1.1.2 Password Verifiers|Add per-password salt before costly hashing to prevent shared passwords from routinely producing identical stored hashes.|Q161157|A password is the secret; salting is a storage-defense transformation of it.|

Authentication rate limiting|facet_or_application|idea|nist|§3.2.2 Rate Limiting|Constrain failed online guesses while balancing attack resistance against legitimate users being locked out.|Q212108|Rate limiting protects the authentication process but is not identity verification itself.|

Replay-resistant authentication|facet_or_application|idea|nist|§3.2.7 Replay Resistance|Use freshness challenges or one-time outputs so recording a past authentication does not enable successful reuse.|Q212108|Freshness protection is a specific authentication property distinct from verifying identity generally.|

Phishing-resistant authentication|facet_or_application|idea|nist|§3.2.5 Phishing Resistance|Bind cryptographic authentication to the real verifier or channel so an impostor cannot relay a reusable output.|Q212108|Verifier binding counters impersonation; it differs from replay resistance, which counters reuse of old messages.|

TLS 1.3|topic|idea|tls|§1.2; §2|Negotiate authenticated encrypted channels using a redesigned handshake that removes static public-key key exchange.|local:authored:000527|A particular protocol version is distinct from the general cryptography field.|Transport Layer Security 1.3

Forward secrecy|idea|idea|tls|Appendix E.1, Forward secret with respect to long-term keys|Keep earlier session keys safe after later long-term-key compromise, subject to the protocol's mode and key-erasure assumptions.|local:authored:000527|This compromise-containment property is narrower than cryptography and is not guaranteed by every TLS mode.|

Grace Hopper|topic|named_subject|hopper|Biography, Harvard and Eckert-Mauchly paragraphs|Connect early compiler work and COBOL standardization to efforts to make programming accessible beyond machine instructions.|Q21198|A particular computing pioneer differs from the scientific field; the source supports technical contributions rather than biography alone.|Grace Murray Hopper

Manchester Baby|topic|named_subject|baby|Collection description, CRT memory and first program paragraphs|See how cathode-ray-tube storage let an experimental 1948 machine hold and run its own program.|Q68|The specific stored-program test machine differs from computers generally and from later commercial designs.|Small-Scale Experimental Machine;SSEM

ENIAC|topic|named_subject|eniac|ENIAC being set up; ENIAC tube change|Explore why electronic calculation speed coexisted with days of wiring and switch-setting for a new problem.|Q169399|Same historical machine; preserve canonical ID and qualify early configuration practice.|

Morris worm|topic|named_subject|morris|Main history, propagation and operational impact paragraphs|See how self-propagating code disrupted network services without destroying stored files in the 1988 incident.|Q3510521|A specific documented security incident and program differs from the general field and other worm senses.|
